# Glenmore: telling you all properly

I have been putting off writing this, which is part of the trouble in the first place.

This blog seemed the best way to say it once, in my own words, to everyone at the same time. That is why Úna set it up all those years ago, so that those of you in Boston, Perth and Leeds, and everyone scattered nearer home, would not have to depend on scraps of news passing from one phone call to another. I should have remembered that before now.

The house in Glenmore is sold, subject to the remaining legal business being completed. The sale was agreed on **3 November**, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**. I am putting the date here plainly because I do not want anybody hearing it second-hand again.

Some of you found out before I had told you properly. That was my fault. I am sorry for it. I am especially sorry to Declan, and I will say more about that further down. I am not apologising for making the decision to sell, because I believe it is the right decision, but I am sorry for the way I handled telling the people I love. There is no point pretending those are the same thing.

I know there will be sadness about this. There may be anger too, and questions about why I did not wait, or why I did not talk it through more widely before agreeing anything. I would rather answer honestly here than defend myself in separate conversations and have slightly different versions travel around the family.

## The house and what it has meant

The house near Oughterard was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. Tom grew up there. For him it was never just an old house with land around it. It was where his people were, where the shape of his childhood remained visible, and where he could go back and stand in a place that knew him before any of the rest of us did.

I have my own history there now.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, naturally, and the cattle were standing around watching us as though they had been invited specially. There was nothing grand about it. I could not have told you then how many times I would go over that small scene in my mind, or how strange it would feel, all these years later, to be making a decision about the place without him.

Our children learned to swim in the lake below the house. I can still see Declan refusing to come out of the water until his lips were blue. He would insist he was not cold, while looking exactly like a child who needed to be taken out immediately and wrapped in a towel. Those summers are not contained in the slates or the walls, I know that. But the house has been the place I could go to stand near them.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out to Glenmore every fortnight. It takes me about forty minutes each way. I air the rooms, check the pipes, look for anything that has got worse since the last visit, and try to keep the place from slipping into complete neglect.

At first, I did it because I could not imagine doing anything else. Going out there felt like something I could still do for Tom. If the windows were opened and the pipes were checked and the place was not left to damp and silence, then some part of our life was still being minded.

But somewhere along the way, the visits changed. Or perhaps I changed, and it took me a while to admit it.

I was no longer going out to a house that felt waiting for life to resume. I was going out to an empty house to carry out a list of jobs, often feeling low before I started the drive home. I would walk through rooms full of memory and then lock the door behind me. Keeping an eye on a place is not the same as living in it. Opening windows is not the same as hearing children downstairs.

## The fall last February

There is something else I have not told you, and I am sorry to be putting it in a blog post after keeping it to myself for so long.

Last February, I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I fell hard, and I lay there for about twenty minutes before I could get up. Nobody was there. I told nobody afterwards.

I can see now that hiding it was foolish. At the time, I did not want the fuss, and I did not want to hear what it might mean. It was easier to treat it as a once-off, to be more careful the next time and say nothing. If I admitted how frightened I had been, I would also have had to admit that I was becoming afraid of being alone at the house.

That fear has not gone away.

I have not fallen again, and this is not a dramatic announcement about my health. But I am seventy-one, and the house is not getting easier to manage while I stand still. Since that morning, I listen differently to quiet, empty places. I think about the frost before I go out. I think about what would happen if I could not get up quickly the next time. Then I drive home and put off thinking properly about what all of that means.

It has been a large part of why I cannot simply leave things as they are.

I should have told the family about the fall when it happened. Instead, I kept one hard thing quiet, and then I kept the growing difficulty of the house quiet, and eventually the news of the sale came out in the worst possible way. That pattern is on me.

## Why I cannot keep maintaining it

Even without the fall, the house needs more than fortnightly visits and good intentions.

Ó Flaithearta’s carried out a roof survey in September. The work on the slates and the back chimney was quoted at **€38,000**. There is also damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing, and that would have to be dealt with in order to sell to anyone in any case.

I am not listing those things to make the house sound worthless, or to suggest that money is the only consideration. It is not. Nor am I saying that nobody, under any circumstances, could take on the work. Someone with the time, money and energy could do it.

But I cannot go on maintaining it as I have been, and I am not able to take on everything it now needs. Another year of checking pipes and opening windows would not change that. Waiting for a summer visit would not change the roof, the damp, the septic tank, or the fact that I am frightened of being there alone after a fall.

There have been days when I thought I should hold on no matter what, simply because letting go felt disloyal. Then there have been other days when I arrived to find another small job waiting and felt overwhelmed before I had taken my coat off. Both feelings are real. Loving a place has not made me better able to look after it.

Over the best part of two years, I have slowly come to understand that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house.

I did not arrive at that neatly. I resisted it for a long time. It sounded like the kind of thing people say when they are trying to make a painful decision sound tidy. But for me it has become true through repetition: going out, opening the house, remembering, feeling his absence, locking up, and driving home. Tom was not being brought nearer by the maintenance. I was only keeping the building from deteriorating as quickly as it otherwise might.

I will always need certain things around me. I am not pretending memories exist in some pure way with no need of objects or places. Anyone who sees what I am keeping will know that. But the house itself does not have to remain mine for Tom to remain part of my life, or part of my children’s lives.

## The people buying it

The sale was agreed with a young couple, Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross. They have two small children, and they want to live in the house. They are not buying it to turn it into a holiday let.

The price they offered was fair. It was lower than an offer from a Dublin buyer in the summer. I took the lower offer deliberately.

I do not want that dressed up as an act of great generosity. I am selling the house, and I am doing so because I have to stop carrying it. I am not a saint for preferring one buyer to another, and choosing a family does not take away whatever grief the sale causes. It was simply the choice I felt best able to live with.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum.

I have thought about that often since Aoife and Kevin told me what they wanted. I can easily imagine him taking satisfaction from the idea of small children being noisy in rooms that have been too quiet. I cannot pretend to know exactly what he would say about every detail of the sale. It would be convenient to recruit him to my side now, and I do not want to do that. But I know he said it, more than once, and it mattered to me when I made the choice.

The Joyces have also said that members of the family are welcome to come out and walk the land any time. I am very grateful for that. Once the house is theirs, it will be their home, and I hope we will respect that, but their kindness means that Glenmore is not suddenly being placed beyond an impenetrable wall.

That invitation will not make everything all right for everyone. I mention it because it is true, and because it is one of the things I want you to hear directly from me rather than as a rumour later.

## Declan

Declan, I want to speak to you directly here, because you read these posts, and because a general apology to “the family” is not enough.

You heard about the sale from your cousin Gráinne on WhatsApp. You did not hear it from me. You rang me at two in the morning, your time, and said I was “selling Dad”.

I said things back to you that I should not have said.

I am not going to repeat the whole argument here or turn it into a public account of who said what. But I will not tidy myself up either. You were hurt and angry, and underneath your anger there was the fact that your father’s home was being sold and you had found out through a message from somebody else. Instead of hearing that properly, I reacted to the accusation. The hour of the call and the strain I was under may explain why I was short-tempered. They do not excuse what I said.

I am sorry.

I regret that I did not consult you before agreeing the sale. You should not have had to absorb the news and the way you learned it at the same time. Whatever my reasons for selling, there was no good reason for leaving you to find out through Gráinne. I should have rung you myself, even if the conversation was going to be difficult. Especially because it was going to be difficult.

At the same time, I am not willing to postpone everything until your summer visit. I want to be honest about that rather than offer a delay I do not believe would change the outcome. Waiting until summer would mean months more of upkeep, expense and worry. It would mean another stretch of driving out and being afraid of finding myself alone there after another fall. It would not make me able to maintain the house.

I know those two statements may sit uncomfortably together: I should have consulted you, and I am not willing to wait. But both are true. I will not pretend I consulted you properly just because I am now explaining myself at length. Nor will I pretend that keeping the house until summer would solve the underlying problem.

You do not have to agree with my decision. You do not have to tell me that you understand before you really do. I would rather you were honest with me than polite for the sake of peace.

I am not angry with you. Not now, and not for what you said on that call. My door is open. You can ring me, or write to me, or come and see me when you are ready. If you want to talk about your Dad without talking about the sale, we can do that too. You have not lost your place with me because we had a terrible argument in the middle of the night.

If you come on 13 December, you will be welcome. If you cannot come, or do not feel able to, that will not be held against you.

## What is staying with the family

I want everyone to know what is being kept.

The dresser is going to Úna’s. Pádraig’s fiddle is staying in the family. I am keeping the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign.

These things matter. I am not clearing Glenmore as though the objects in it were just a problem to be disposed of. The dresser, the fiddle and the lamp have all been part of the life around the house. The photographs hold faces and days that cannot be replaced. The gate sign belongs to the story too, which is why I could not leave it behind as though it were a piece of old timber.

I know a list of keepsakes will not answer the loss of a house. It would be insulting to say, in effect, that we are keeping the lamp and therefore nothing important is changing. A great deal is changing. I only want to be clear that the things named here are not being sold, thrown out or forgotten in the confusion.

There will be work involved in clearing and sorting, and I would rather do that with family where possible than treat it as a private administrative task. No one has to pretend to enjoy it. I do not expect to enjoy much of it myself.

## Sunday, 13 December

Before the house is cleared, I would like us to have a family day out there on **Sunday, 13 December 2026**.

Anyone who can come is welcome. We will have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, especially if you want to go down towards the lake or walk any of the land. Come for the whole day or for whatever part of it suits you.

There will be no formal programme. I am not asking everyone to stand up and make a speech about Glenmore, though if somebody wants to tell a story, I will be glad to hear it. We can walk, look through the place, talk, argue a little if necessary, and remember Tom without having to make the day perfect.

Children are welcome too. I would like that very much. It would be good to have the sound of them there once more before the house passes to Aoife and Kevin and their children begin making their own life in it.

If you are in Boston, Perth or Leeds and cannot make the journey, please do not feel that your absence will be read as a lack of love. Distance is real, and December is not easy for everyone. The invitation is open to those who can manage it, not a test for those who cannot.

I hope Declan will feel able to come, but I mean what I said above: there will be no ill will if he does not.

## The date, and what comes after

So that there is no uncertainty, the sale of the Glenmore house is due to close on **15 January 2027**. That is the date everyone should have. If anything material changes, I will tell people directly rather than leave them to pick it up from somebody else.

Until then, there is December, and the clearing to be done, and time to gather what we are keeping. After January, I will still have Tom’s proposal in the rainy haggard, with the cattle looking on. I will still have the picture of the children in the lake, and Declan insisting he was fine while turning blue. I will still have Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the lamp and the rest.

That may sound as though I am trying to convince myself. Perhaps I am, a little. Understanding something and finding it painless are not the same thing.

I expect to grieve the house. I expect there will be days when I wonder whether I should have found another way. I may drive near it some day and feel a fresh shock that I no longer have the key. I am not going to pretend that because the decision is right, it has stopped hurting.

But I am also tired of being frightened at the thought of going there alone. I am tired of measuring my love for Tom in pipes checked and windows opened. The house needs children and daily life and people with the energy to repair what is failing. It should not be kept empty so that I can continue proving, visit by visit, that I have not forgotten him.

I am sorry for the silence, and for the confused and hurtful way the news reached some of you. I am not going to say there was no other way I could have handled it, because plainly there was. After all my years as a teacher telling children that it is better to say the difficult thing plainly, I managed to avoid my own advice for far too long.

Please come on Sunday, 13 December, if you can. Have soup, bring your wellies, and walk the place with me. Bring your memories too, including the awkward ones. There is room for all of them.

And Declan, I mean this without conditions: I am not angry. The door is open.
